verdict: DEFER (full text inaccessible to this environment; provisional lean REJECT/low-value ENRICH). On the abstract alone the paper is a historical-institutionalist sociology of platform monopolization with no evident land or rent content; no anchor sentence in the existing wiki pages can be grounded in anything beyond the abstract. If a later pass obtains the full text (e.g. the person downloads the open-access PDF) and finds a rent passage, the only plausible target is concepts/data-rents.md (section 'Why It's the Steepest Part of the Gradient', as one bullet beside 'The rent reading' / 'The efficiency counter') with the proposed anchor sentence: 'Wu defines extraction as the microeconomist's monopoly rent, and his evidence is largely illustrative, so the book states the case rather than measuring it; see Rentier for the argument and its critics.[4]' -- a Beyer sentence would follow it as a third origin-of-concentration account (historical sequence rather than network effects as natural monopoly). Do not publish anything from the abstract alone beyond, at most, a one-sentence abstract-level mention (A-claim only as 'the abstract states').
claim_grade: B for what the abstract states about the argument (open metadata, peer-reviewed Springer journal; Tier 1 under §4c: Beyer is a sociology professor at Universität Hamburg per scanner; not listed in sources/audit/people-tiers.json, judged by rubric as recognised scholar; affiliation NOT independently verified, Crossref author record has empty affiliation). D (unknown) for every item the brief asked about that the abstract does not cover: parasitic-extension specifics, rent language, firm figures, policy conclusions.

verified_from_abstract_(Crossref): Premise: 'The internet economy is characterized by the pervasive dominance of digital monopolies such as Alphabet, Meta and Uber' (abstract; note Amazon is not named in the abstract).

Ahistorical explanations named: external network effects, economies of scale, technological barriers to entry, user lock-in, inadequate antitrust regulation. He grants they 'may accurately describe the current situation' but are 'insufficient to fully account for the emergence of digital monopolies' (abstract).

Two historical conditions: 'the internet's legacy as a non-commercial infrastructure, combined with users' initial reluctance to pay for online services', which 'created market conditions in which network effects became particularly significant' (abstract). So network effects are a consequence, not the primary cause.

Downstream consequences claimed: 'the emergence of multi-sided digital platforms, the growing separation of use value from exchange value, and the parasitic extension of digital market logic into the offline economy' (abstract). The abstract gives no more than this phrase; what 'parasitic extension' refers to is therefore UNVERIFIED (reference list hints at Amazon marketplace/third-party sellers, Uber offline services, but this is inference).
Conclusion: digital monopolization is 'not the outcome of network effects culminating in natural monopoly' but 'a historically specific sequence' contingent on context (abstract; paraphrase).

Reference list (86) hints at engagement with: Sadowski 2020 'The Internet of Landlords: Digital Platforms and New Mechanisms of Rentier Capitalism' (Antipode); Mazzucato 2018 value creation vs value extraction; Birch & Muniesa 2020 Assetization; Rikap 2021; Srnicek 2017; Zuboff 2019; Hagiu & Wright 2015; Rysman 2009; Katz & Shapiro 1985; Sharkey 1983 (natural monopoly); Kirchner & Beyer 2016 (his own platform-logic paper); Klinge et al. 2023; Marx Kapital vol. 1 (use/exchange value); market-share sources (Amazon 56.7% US e-commerce 2021 via PYMNTS; Uber 71% US ride-share 2022 via Zippia; Amazon third-party seller share via Statista; StatCounter). These are citations only; how Beyer uses them is unverified.

Existence of a rent discussion: UNVERIFIED. Citation of Sadowski, Mazzucato and Birch & Muniesa suggests a brief rent/extraction mention, but nothing confirms 'rent', 'monopoly rent' or 'economic rent' is used.
not_obtainable: Section/page-located quotations, figures for Alphabet/Amazon/Meta/Uber, policy conclusions, the 'parasitic extension' definition.

title: How a Property Tax Rate Gets Set (Economy in Context, 8 Nov 2026, part 1 of 2)
what_was_fetched: Read in full (27 KB HTML, ~17 KB text): item2-article-text.txt (raw: item2-article.html). Publisher pages read in full: item2-about-economyincontext.txt (/articles/about.html, ‘About This Site’; the /about.html path scanned from the nav returned 404, then the site's own link was used) and item2-how-site-is-paid-for.txt. Primaries fetched (ordinary requests, all HTTP 200): Texas Comptroller truth-in-taxation page (item2-texas-truth-in-taxation.txt; item2-texas-tin-index.txt is a duplicate of the www. variant), Georgia HB 92 (2025) signed text (item2-georgia-hb92.txt, PDF in dl2/), Georgia SB 566 (2026) signed text (item2-georgia-sb566.txt), Georgia Rule 560-11-2-.58 via Cornell LII (item2-georgia-rule-560-11-2-58.txt), Utah HB 236 (2026) enrolled PDF (item2-utah-hb236.txt, amends 59-2-919), Florida Stat. 200.069 (item2-florida-200-069.txt). Partial/unusable: Texas statutes site Tax Code ch. 26 (JS shell, 1.4 KB, item2-texas-tax-code-26-04.txt) and le.utah.gov 59-2-919 page (JS shell; no statute text; the enrolled HB 236 carries the amended section instead). Not fetched: Florida SB 4-F analysis, Ohio LSC triennial update, Cook County pages, CBS Miami, Coastal Courier, Kem Gardner brief (not needed for the verdict).
verdict: REJECT as a source (Tier 2/3 anonymous one-person site; never cite for support). OPTIONAL ENRICH, cited to statutes only: events/proposition-13.md (a sentence glossing the Lincoln explainer's 'a silent tax increase' passage in the paragraph beginning 'A Lincoln Institute explainer published in October 2026...') and/or places/texas.md (section 'The 3.5 Percent Revenue Cap and Tax-Rate Elections', which already uses 'no-new-revenue' without defining it). Anchor in events/proposition-13.md: 'describes a locality that leaves its rate unchanged as values rise as producing "a silent tax increase".[15]'. Proposed addition (to be cited to Texas Comptroller and Georgia Rule 560-11-2-.58 / HB 92, not to the explainer): in Texas the no-new-revenue rate is 'generally equal to last year's taxes divided by the current taxable value of properties that were also on the tax roll last year' (Texas Comptroller, Truth-in-Taxation page), and Georgia defines its rollback rate as 'the previous year's millage rate plus or minus the millage equivalent of the total net assessed value added to or deducted by reassessments of existing real property' (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 560-11-2-.58(i)); an adopted rate above it is advertised as a tax increase. The arithmetic example (500M digest, 10 mills, 8% reassessment, 10M new construction) is the explainer's own illustration; the wiki can use its own numbers but should not borrow the 9.26 vs 10 mill figures as sourced fact.
claim_grade: Explainer: C for any factual statement standing alone, §4c Tier 2 at best (anonymous operator; scanner's 'professional ... project' is wrong). Statutes and Comptroller page: A, Tier 1 official bodies. Explainer arithmetic: checked and correct (below), so the mechanism claims are reliable, but this does not raise its tier.

content_summary.publisher_facts: About page: 'One person, who has chosen not to be named', no byline, site 'went up in October 2026', no sponsors ('takes no money from any party, campaign, company or advocacy group'); paid out of pocket, about $2,430 a year ($30 domains plus about $200 a month 'research tools'), hosted free on GitHub static pages; weekly Buttondown email; contact hello@economyincontext.org; CC BY 4.0 with credit. The About page logs its own corrections (e.g. 31 Oct 2026 jobs 'fastest on record' claim; 30 Oct 2026 rent index 41% vs 36%; several wrong figures in other articles within its first weeks), showing a self-corrected but very new site. Quote (About, 'Who is behind it'): 'One person, who has chosen not to be named.'
content_summary.logic: Rate is 'the last number decided': local government sets levy, assessor sets the (net) digest, rate roughly = levy / net digest; rate x net digest = levy. 'Mill' = $1 per $1,000 of taxable value (10 mills = 1%), stated correctly. Georgia taxes 40% of market value; digest = tax roll = grand list; gross vs net digest.
content_summary.rollback_mechanism: When values rise, same rate brings in more; many states require calculating a rollback / rolled-back / no-new-revenue rate that yields about last year's money from the same properties. Adopting a higher rate counts as a tax increase; triggers notices, hearings, in Texas sometimes an election. It holds the total, not individual bills (burden shifts to homes that gained most, and from non-revalued classes to revalued ones).
content_summary.worked_example_verified: Net digest $500M, 10 mills = $5.0M. Existing property +8% (+$40M) plus $10M new construction = $550M. At 10 mills: $5.5M (+10%). Rollback = $5.0M / $540M = 9.259 mills (article: about 9.26); at 9.26 mills on $550M = $5.09M (+1.9%, the extra about $93,000 from new construction). At 9.6 mills = $5.28M (+5.6%). Georgia-style subtraction: 10 mills x 40/550 = 0.727, giving about 9.27 mills (article: about 9.27). Three-homes table ($204k, $216k, $230k at 9.26 mills = $1,889, $2,000, $2,130) and the homes-versus-business split (homes $250M to $290M; $232,000 home pays $2,148, business $200,000 pays $1,852; homes' share 50% to about 54%) all recomputed and correct. The town is made up.
state_examples_as_the_article_states_the: Georgia: advertise 'notice of property tax increase', press release, three hearings (Georgia DOR); 2025 assessment notices show estimated rollback rate, bill must say in bold if adopted rate exceeds it (HB 92, 2025); 2026 law repeals yearly certification of that estimate, 2026 notices list exemptions and estimated savings (SB 566, 2026; Coastal Courier).

Florida: since June 2026 a city or county may adopt up to the rolled-back rate by simple majority; up to 10% above by two-thirds; more by unanimity (three-fourths if nine or more members) or referendum (CS/SB 4-F; CBS Miami).
Texas: most cities and counties adopting a rate above the voter-approval rate (about 3.5% more operating revenue plus debt) must put it to an election (Texas Comptroller).

Utah: notice by mail or advertisement and a public hearing for rates above the certified rate; 2026 law adds an earlier announcement for July budget-year governments and requires the extra revenue be set aside (Kem Gardner Policy Institute via Utah Business; HB 236).

Ohio: counties reappraise every six years with a three-year statistical update (Ohio LSC); Cook County reassesses one-third each year; 2025 north suburban appeals cut commercial values 14%, homes' share of assessed value 66% to 68% (Cook County Assessor).

primary_checks.texas: Texas Comptroller page (item2-texas-truth-in-taxation.txt, 'Truth-in-Taxation'): confirms 'The no-new-revenue tax rate enables the public to evaluate the relationship between taxes for the prior year and for the current year, based on a tax rate that would produce the same amount of taxes if applied to the same properties taxed in both years' and the 'last year's taxes divided by the current taxable value of properties that were also on the tax roll last year' formula; voter-approval rate gives the previous year's operating revenue plus an extra 3.5 percent (8 percent for special taxing units), plus debt; election required if the adopted rate exceeds the voter-approval rate. Matches explainer. Note the Comptroller page says elections apply to 'most taxing units'; explainer's 'most cities and counties' is a fair compression (school districts follow different rules; places/texas.md already notes the 30,000-population threshold for municipalities under §26.07, a nuance the explainer omits).
primary_checks.georgia: Rule 560-11-2-.58(i) (LII): rollback rate = previous year's millage plus or minus the millage equivalent of net assessed value added or deducted by reassessments of existing real property; calculated for counties by the tax commissioner, for municipalities by the tax collector. HB 92 (2025) signed text and SB 566 (2026) signed text both contain the 'estimated roll-back rate' provisions (HB 92 line 49 definition; bold 'The adopted millage rate exceeds the estimated roll-back rate as stated in the annual notice of assessment' wording). SB 566 section 7 repeal of certification: explainer's claim not independently confirmed line by line (text saved for a fixer to check). O.C.G.A. 48-5-32.1 itself NOT fetched (Justia 403); LII rule fetched instead.
primary_checks.florida: Fla. Stat. 200.069 (notice of proposed property taxes) fetched; CS/SB 4-F text and analysis not fetched, so the 2026 vote thresholds are explainer-only here.
primary_checks.utah: Enrolled HB 236 (2026) fetched; it amends 59-2-919 (notice and public hearing for certain tax increases) and defines 'truth-in-taxation exemption period'; the le.utah.gov code page is a JS shell so the unamended statute text is not saved. Explainer's HB 236 claims not verified line by line.

'no-new-revenue' appears only in places/texas.md (section 3.5 Percent Revenue Cap, citing Tax Code §26.04/§26.07, with a per-acre table at the no-new-revenue rate) without being explained as a concept; 'mills' appears in places/pittsburgh.md as the land/building rate. events/proposition-13.md carries the Lincoln Land Lines explainer (source 15, Jon Gorey, 21 Oct 2026) 'silent tax increase' phrase, the NACo count, and the Iowa SF 2472 levy-limit formula (102 per cent levy formula, new-valuation exclusion; source 21) with Tax Foundation as Tier 2 origin-only (source 22).
